source: Finke & Slayton (1988) Explorations of creative visual synthesis in mental imagery, Experiment 1
finding: Founding parts-to-pattern paradigm. Students got three randomly chosen parts (shapes, lines, letters), closed their eyes, and had 2 minutes to imagine them into a nameable figure. No target, no instruction on how to combine. A naive experimenter guessed in advance what they would make.
numbers: N=39 students, 8 trials each, 312 trials. Recognizable pattern on 119 trials (38.1%); 19 judged highly creative. Poor correspondence 32.7%, wrong parts 6.7%, no pattern 22.4%. 56 distinct pattern types. 37 of 39 made at least one pattern; 12 made at least one creative one. Experimenter predicted only 14.3% of recognizable patterns and 1 of the 19 creative ones. 74.4% of subjects named trial-and-error assembly as main strategy; they produced 18 of the 19 creative patterns.
quote: discoveries in imagery can be reliably induced under appropriate laboratory conditions
limits: Parts from a 15-item set weighted to simple forms; creative status judged by 3 judges (rating 4+ of 5 plus 2 of 3 labelling it creative); no control without parts; undergraduates only; strategy was self-report.
agent_relevance: Generate-first is cheap and productive: undirected trial-and-error combination yields a nameable structure about 4 trials in 10, and the outcome cannot be predicted from the parts. Supports a wide undirected generation stage before any target is fixed (S3 open mode).

source: Finke & Slayton (1988) Explorations of creative visual synthesis in mental imagery, Experiment 2
finding: Subjects first guessed what patterns others could make from a part set, then did the imagery task. Their own guesses did not predict their discoveries, and prior guessing did not help.
numbers: N=70 students. 280 trials repeated from the guessing phase: 124 recognizable (44.3%), 19 creative (15.3% of recognizable). 280 non-guessed trials: 110 recognizable (39.3%), 15 creative; poor correspondence 44.6%, wrong parts 11.1%, none 5.0%. Subjects predicted only 18.5% of their own recognizable patterns; chi-square(1)<1 against experimenter. Guessing vs not guessing: chi-square(1)=1.44, ns. Across both experiments: 353 recognizable patterns, 53 judged highly creative; 67 of 70 made at least one pattern, 26 made at least one creative one.
limits: Same part set and judges as Experiment 1; the figure that only 10.0% were predicted when all three guesses were made is a small-cell figure.
agent_relevance: A model cannot reliably predict from the parts which combination will pay off. This argues for sampling combinations and checking them by running (G8) instead of choosing by reasoning about which will be good.

source: Finke & Slayton (1988) Explorations of creative visual synthesis in mental imagery, authors' interpretation
finding: Authors separate creative combination of parts from creative interpretation of the combination, and say theories of imagery must explain how features are combined, not only retrieved. Discoveries came from trial-and-error assembly until a form 'emerged'.
numbers: Examples: bug, bowling ball, ice cream soda, firecracker from sets such as letter V, C and O. In some the arrangement was clever; in others the reading of the arrangement was clever.
quote: distinguish between creative combinations of parts and creative interpretations of those combinations
limits: Interpretation of mechanism is by the authors, based on a self-report questionnaire (74.4% trial-and-error).
agent_relevance: Two separate slots in our schema: one that builds a structure (S3) and one that reads meaning into it (S4/S5 explore). The two can be run and scored separately.

source: Finke (1990) Creative Imagery: Discoveries and Inventions in Visualization, preinventive-form invention task, as described in Preis (undergraduate honors thesis, UC San Diego)
finding: Secondary description of the core Geneplore paradigm. Subject picks or is given 3 of 15 object parts, mentally builds a preinventive form, draws it, is then given one of 8 semantic categories (furniture, tools, weapons, toys and so on) and must say what the form is and how it works in that category. Finke's reported result: highly creative inventions were most common when subjects chose their own parts and the experimenter chose the category. In a spanning variant (one form, eight categories) the second function was the hardest to generate.
numbers: Parts: 15. Categories: 8. Practice categories: personal items, appliances. The spanning variant is described as not implemented empirically by Finke; the 'second function hardest' point is his subjective note.
limits: Thesis is not peer reviewed and gives Finke's results only second hand; exact percentages from the 1990 book were not available to us. Year of the thesis not recorded.
agent_relevance: Gives the exact task structure to mimic in an LLM test: build a form from parts first, hide the target category, then reveal it.

source: Preis (undergraduate honors thesis, UC San Diego) Does labelling preinventive forms cause functional fixedness?
finding: Small extension of the spanning task: naming a preinventive form before generating functions did not significantly change the time to produce new functions. Time per function fell over the six functions.
numbers: Mean spanning time naming condition 21.4 s (SD 18.5) vs non-naming about the same (0.2 s difference), not significant. First six trials only: naming 23.8 s vs non-naming 29.6 s, ns. Fatigue effect: times decreased significantly from the first to last function.
limits: Small undergraduate study, sample size not recorded in our read.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence that labelling a structure early does not by itself lock it. Do not treat as a settled result.

source: McKnight, Ormerod, Sas & Dix (2006) As useful as a bicycle to a fish: exploration versus constraint in creativity (Cognitive Science Society)
finding: First within-experiment replication of Finke (1990) Experiments 2 and 6, preinventive phase versus control. Preinventive phase (build a form first, then get the category) gave more original but less practical designs, and no gain in overall creativity. Mental and physical (dough) synthesis did not differ in creativity.
numbers: N=48 students, 6 trials each, 288 trials; 21 failures (11 control, 10 preinventive conversion). Originality: preinventive 2.47 vs control 2.23, F(1,46)=3.47, p<.07. Practicality: 3.08 vs 3.32, F(1,46)=4.38, p=.04. Sum (creativity) score: no significant effects. 'Highly creative' (score above 7): 22 of 267 designs (8.24%), 13 preinventive vs 9 control. No design reached Finke's cut-off of 8.
quote: a preinventive phase does not enhance the exploration of novel combinations but instead increases the degree of design constraint
limits: Finke's rating scales and judge training were not fully published, so this is a close but not exact replication; independent judges' reliability was low (alpha .55 originality, .44 practicality, .57 creativity; knowledgeable judges .73, .70, .37); students not experts.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for our Geneplore question (b): generating a structure before the constraint is shown raises novelty but lowers practicality, with no net gain. Expect the same trade in an LLM test and score the two separately (G8).

source: McKnight et al. (2006), critique of Finke's design and theory
finding: Authors list weaknesses of the original studies: effects came from cross-experiment comparisons, not within-experiment tests; two 'trained' judges with no published reliability or training details; results only in book chapters; Finke's task runs one generate-then-explore pass and does not test the cycle the model claims. Two rival accounts: exploration (preinventive phase should raise both originality and practicality) versus constraint (originality up, practicality down). Their data fit constraint.
numbers: Prior physical-synthesis work: Pike (2002) found a preinventive phase gave more creative products, but participants were told about creativity and were not blind; Ishii and Miwa (2002) used LEGO Mindstorms, which constrain materials.
limits: Single lab, students; the constraint account is an interpretation, not a direct test.
agent_relevance: Treat Geneplore's gain as an unproven claim in our design list. The reliable part is the trade (novelty up, practicality down).

source: McKnight et al. (2006), statement of the Geneplore model
finding: Compact statement of the theory: generation (retrieval, association, synthesis, transformation, analogical transfer) produces preinventive structures; exploration (attribute discovery and assignment, conceptual interpretation, functional inference) interprets them; product constraints focus or expand the concept and the loop repeats. Model is prescriptive, with no built-in limit on the type of creativity.
numbers: Figure 1 of the paper: boxes for generation of preinventive structures, preinventive exploration and interpretation, and focus or expand concept, with product constraints acting on the loop.
limits: Secondary statement of the 1992 model; no formal or computational version exists in the sources opened here.
agent_relevance: Maps to S3 (generate) then S4/S5 (interpret and revise) with constraints as the test. The model is a verbal flow chart, not a program, so our code must supply the rules.

source: Smith, Ward & Schumacher (1993) Constraining effects of examples in a creative generation task, Experiment 1
finding: Showing three example designs that share features makes later 'new' designs copy those features, even though output quantity is unchanged. Task: draw as many new toys or new creatures for an uninhabited planet as possible in 20 minutes, with existing ones not allowed. Examples (ball toys; creatures with four legs, antennae, tail) were shown 90 s and removed.
numbers: N=94. Mean toys per person 2.82 (control) vs 2.90 (examples); creatures 2.95 vs 3.08; no difference. Toy features: ball .11 vs .31; physical activity .23 vs .39. Toy overall conformity .22 control vs .35 examples. Creatures: antennae .05 vs .17; tail .15 vs .37; overall conformity .11 vs .24. A reported F(1,92)=8.13 tests overall conformity (listed after the toy analysis).
limits: Which F belongs to toys or creatures follows text order and was not rechecked against the table; 'conformity' counts only the planted features, not total originality; student sample; Marsh et al. (1996) later found no loss of total output.
agent_relevance: Warns against placing a prior solution in the generator's context before open generation: the model's new ideas will inherit its features. Keep S3 open mode free of shown examples.

source: Smith, Ward & Schumacher (1993) Constraining effects of examples in a creative generation task, Experiments 2 and 3
finding: Conformity did not significantly fall after a 23-minute delay. It was not caused by subjects assuming they should copy: telling them to be very different from the examples did not reduce conformity, and telling them to conform raised it.
numbers: Experiment 2 N=91 (immediate vs 23-min delay, examples vs control). Experiment 3 had four groups (control, standard examples, examples/conform, examples/diverge), df 76 so about 80 subjects. Standard vs conform: t(76)=3.36 (conform higher). Standard vs diverge: t(76)=1.33, ns. Group effects: tail F(3,76)=9.27; four legs F(3,76)=4.26; antennae F(3,76)=1.08, ns.
quote: explicitly instructing subjects to create ideas that were very different from the examples did not decrease conformity
limits: Delay effect is a non-significant decrease, not shown to be stable; 23 min is short; three examples with shared features is a strong manipulation.
agent_relevance: Telling a model 'do not copy the example' is not a fix. Remove the example from context or check output against it by code (G3, G8).

source: Marsh, Landau & Hicks (1996) How examples may (and may not) constrain creativity, Experiment 1
finding: Replicated conformity and showed it grows with the number of examples. But total output, design elaborateness and noncritical features did not shrink, so the claim that examples reduce creativity was not confirmed.
numbers: About 80 participants (df 4,75), 0, 1, 3, 6 or 9 example creatures, 25 min. Conformity: .087, .137, .189, .233, .280. Creatures per person 4.4, 5.1, 4.9, 5.2, 5.4. Features per creature 6.6, 6.3, 6.9, 7.8, 7.1. Share of critical features .044 to .121; common features .807 to .674; novel features .056 to .053; uncommon features .083 to .147.
limits: One task, drawing creatures; novelty measured by feature coding, not human originality ratings, in Experiment 1.
agent_relevance: Copying is a real effect but costs less than first thought: it adds feature overlap without lowering volume or novelty. Count overlap with shown examples in code as a diversity signal, not as a failure.

source: Marsh, Landau & Hicks (1996) How examples may (and may not) constrain creativity, Experiments 2 and 3
finding: Examples that bundle naturally uncorrelated features (antennae with claws) were copied as a bundle and the abstract reports greater rated creativity. A one-day delay increased conformity, as models of inadvertent plagiarism predict, which activation-decay accounts do not.
numbers: Experiment 2 about 77 participants (df 2,74): natural-bundle examples (four legs plus tail) gave more tail-and-legs creatures, omnibus F(2,74)=5.18, p<.01; artificial-bundle examples gave more antennae-and-claws, F(2,74)=4.50, p<.01. Experiment 3 about 75 participants (36 immediate): conformity .169 immediate vs .242 after one-day delay, F(1,73)=4.74, p<.05; total creatures 5.47 vs 5.03; critical-feature share .078 vs .115.
limits: Few creativity raters; the 'do not copy' admonition might itself cue the examples (authors argue against, citing Smith et al.).
agent_relevance: Delay does not wash out exposure: a stale earlier attempt kept in a long context can still shape new ideas. Restarts that drop earlier attempts are cleaner than reminders.

source: Marsh, Landau & Hicks (1996) How examples may (and may not) constrain creativity, theory section (activation, retrieval blocking, category abstraction)
finding: Four accounts compared: activation of example features, retrieval blocking, Ward's structured imagination, and a new category-abstraction account in which examples redefine the category of acceptable new exemplars. The rise in conformity after delay fits plagiarism-style accounts and not blocking. Authors note people define a creature with a stable five or six features.
numbers: The recall experiment that would show what people retain from the examples has not been done, per the authors.
limits: Mechanism claims untested; presented as candidate accounts.
agent_relevance: Suggests the generator abstracts a category from what it sees. If the context defines what a new idea looks like, samples stay inside it; vary the framing, not only the temperature.

source: Ward (1994) Structured imagination: the role of category structure in exemplar generation (Cognitive Psychology 27, 1-40), as described by Marsh et al. (1996) and Sowden et al. (2015)
finding: Four experiments: students imagined creatures for a new planet. They started from Earth animals, so creations had bilateral symmetry, sense organs and limbs. When the planet was made harsh (molten lava), they added wings rather than features from non-animal categories like jet engines. Instruction to create creatures 'beyond their wildest imagination' did not remove the pattern. Ward calls this the path of least resistance.
numbers: Exact counts per feature not obtained: the primary paper is paywalled and secondary sources give no percentages. Lava is Experiment 3.
limits: Primary paper not opened; second-hand account only. Figures must come from the original before being cited.
agent_relevance: Describes the default of any generator: start from the typical category member and modify it. Open-mode generation needs a forced departure (a constraint that breaks the template, or a different seed category).

source: Christensen & Schunn (2007) The relationship of analogical distance to analogical function and preinventive structure: the case of engineering design (Memory & Cognition 35, 29-38)
finding: Field test of the preinventive-structure idea in real engineering design meetings (in vivo). Designers used analogies often, and the kind depended on the form the idea took: unsupported ideas drew more distant (between-domain) analogies than physical prototypes, in line with exemplar fixation. Analogies had three jobs: identify a problem, solve it, explain a concept.
numbers: 7 transcripts, 102 analogy segments (11.3 per hour). 55% within-domain, 45% between-domain. Ideas (N=64 segments), sketches (N=8), prototypes (N=30). Ideas had more analogies than prototypes, chi-square(1)=7.88, p=.006. Distance vs structure: chi-square(2)=19.26, p<.001; ideas produced more between-domain analogies than prototypes (Fisher p<.001; sketches vs prototypes p=.019). Functions: 28% identify problems, 40% solve, 32% explain. Within-domain analogies shared 3.82 of 4 surface features vs 0.52 for between-domain, t(100)=17.21. 96% of designers use sketches or models (survey cited from Romer et al.).
limits: One medical-plastics firm, observational; order and stage confounds checked but not removed.
agent_relevance: Concrete artifacts pull thinking toward near analogies. Keep abstract low-commitment structures alive in S3 and delay the concrete draft.

source: Jansson & Smith (1991) design fixation vs Purcell & Gero (1992) failed replication, as reported in Christensen & Schunn (2007)
finding: Design fixation (copying features of a shown example) was found with mechanical engineering students and professionals, but Purcell and Gero (1992) failed to replicate. Dahl and Moreau (2002) did find transfer of example properties and fewer distant analogies after a sketch of a drive-in window tray was shown.
numbers: No numbers given in the paper for these studies.
limits: Second-hand one-sentence report; the failed replication is flagged, not described.
agent_relevance: Fixation by examples is not universal. Test it on our own tasks before building a guard around it.

source: Sowden, Pringle & Gabora (2015) The shifting sands of creative thinking: connections to dual process theory (Thinking & Reasoning 21, 40-60)
finding: Maps Geneplore onto dual-process theory: generation is Type 1 (fast, associative) and exploration is Type 2 (analytic), but analytic thought can also create new ideas (Finke 1996), so generation involves both and exploration only Type 2. Notes that Blind Variation and Selective Retention assumes independent successive ideas, which the Geneplore view does not.
numbers: No new data; review only. Cites Mednick's flat vs steep associative hierarchies and Howard-Jones's dual-state model.
limits: The Type 1 and Type 2 mapping is the authors' reading; they say creative work does not map straight onto dual-process models.
agent_relevance: Our S3 sample is Type-1-like and our S4 test is Type-2-like. Good fit, but the model can also generate by analysis, so do not assume the sample step is always random.

source: Peeperkorn, Kouwenhoven, Brown & Jordanous (2024) Is temperature the creativity parameter of large language models?
finding: Test of the 'randomness equals creativity' claim for the generate step. Llama-2-chat 70B wrote stories at seven temperatures; humans rated novelty, typicality, cohesion and coherence. Temperature raised novelty weakly and reduced coherence moderately; no effect on cohesion or typicality.
numbers: 36 non-expert participants, 100 stories generated, 31 rated (5 per temperature plus an exemplar), at least 5 ratings per story. Novelty vs temperature beta=.308, SE=.138, Rc2=.385 (p<.05). Incoherence vs temperature beta=.240, SE=.122, Rc2=.646 (p<.05). Mean novelty rating 3.12; mean incoherence 2.13 (lower is more coherent). Inter-rater Cronbach alpha averaged .639 (novelty alone .547). Normalised edit distance vs novelty beta=2.01 (p<.01).
limits: One model, one prompt, one short story task; 31 stories; low rater agreement; novelty measured relative to a greedy exemplar.
agent_relevance: Raising temperature is a weak way to get more novel structures and it costs coherence. Better to vary the seed, constraint or operator than only the temperature (G12).

source: Si, Yang & Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: Best-measured generate-then-filter LLM pipeline. It generated many seed ideas, removed near duplicates, then ranked them with an LLM pairwise tournament. Blind expert review found the LLM ideas more novel than expert-written ideas, slightly weaker on feasibility, and not clearly better overall.
numbers: 49 human ideas, 49 AI ideas, 49 AI ideas with human rerank. 79 reviewers, 298 reviews. Novelty mean: human 4.84 (119 reviews), AI 5.64 (109), AI plus human rerank 5.81 (109); p<.01 and p<.001 in the review-level test. Overall score: human 4.68, AI 4.85 (p=1.00), rerank 5.34 (p=.04). Pipeline: 4000 seeds per topic, cosine threshold 0.8 for deduplication, Swiss-system pairwise ranker with N=5 rounds.
limits: Prompt-based NLP ideas only; ideas not executed, so novelty is rated, not tested; the authors warn human novelty judgement is hard. Review count and idea count differ between analyses.
agent_relevance: Gives a measured example of the generate step (wide sampling) paying off in novelty with little gain in overall quality. In our case the filter must be a run test, not an LLM ranker (G8).

source: Si et al. (2024), diversity and evaluation failures of the pipeline
finding: Two weak points of generate-then-filter. First, sampling more stops adding new ideas: duplicates dominate. Second, LLM judges agree with expert ranking no better than experts agree with each other, and in fact worse.
numbers: Of 4000 seed ideas per topic only about 5% (about 200) remained after deduplication. Judge accuracy against expert top and bottom 25%: best LLM evaluator (Claude 3.5 pairwise) 53.3% vs inter-reviewer consistency 56.1%; GPT-4o direct 50.0, GPT-4o pairwise 45.0; Claude 3.5 direct 51.7; AI Scientist reviewer 43.3. On ICLR data the same kind of ranker scored 71.4 to 71.9%.
limits: Accuracy measured only against the 25% extremes; the table was garbled in text extraction, so recheck the label-to-number mapping before citing.
agent_relevance: Confirms G8 and G12: sample widely only until duplicates saturate, and do not trust a model to pick the winner.

source: Palmiero, Nori, Aloisi, Ferrara & Piccardi (2015) Domain-specificity of creativity: visual creativity and visual mental imagery (Frontiers in Psychology 6:1870)
finding: Used Finke's creative synthesis task to ask who makes good preinventive forms. Spatial transformation ability (paper folding) predicted originality of inventions; imagery vividness predicted lower practicality. Models for the originality of preinventive forms themselves were not significant.
numbers: N=50 college students, six triads, 15 s memorize, 2 min combine, 1 min describe. Paper Folding vs originality of inventions r=.41; vs originality of preinventive forms r=.37. Vividness (VVIQ) vs practicality r=-.33. Regression for invention originality R2=31.5% (visualization style beta=.420, p<.01; Paper Folding beta=.325, p<.05). Judge reliability ICC about .48 to .58.
limits: Small sample, two judges, one task format, novices only; the paper's text has sign and R2 inconsistencies; read through a fetch summary, not a clean PDF.
agent_relevance: Individual differences sit in the exploration step (spatial transformation, interpretation) more than in building the form. Suggests the strength to add is interpret-and-transform (S4/S5), not more sampling.

source: Finke (1990) via teaching slides 'Creative invention task'
finding: Slides report that combining parts intuitively with no use in mind worked best, that people found more creative uses for forms they built themselves than for forms built by others, and that knowing the category first and reshaping the form to fit may not be most creative.
numbers: No numbers on the slides.
limits: Slides are unsourced and give no figures; low weight. The Colorado CreativeIT page returned a server error and was not read.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as McKnight: withhold the target while building. Needs a direct test.

source: Gu, Wang, Zhang & Li (2024) LLMs can realize combinatorial creativity: generating creative ideas via LLMs for scientific research
finding: A pipeline that retrieves concepts at several abstraction levels from other domains, then systematically recombines components, based on Boden's combinatorial creativity. Reports closer match to later real research developments than baselines.
numbers: Reported gain of 7 to 10% in similarity scores across several metrics on the OAG-Bench dataset (from the abstract; tables not extracted).
limits: Only abstract and introduction read; outcome measured as similarity to real later work, a proxy for usefulness, not a novelty test; Boden's framework, not Geneplore, is the stated base.
agent_relevance: Close in structure to Geneplore's retrieve, associate, synthesize loop; shows a combine step that is explicit and not left to the model's own pick.

source: Bi, Ma & Hua (2026) A Geneplore model-based taxonomy of digital tools for supporting creative design processes (AHFE)
finding: Systematic review that sorts 57 creativity support tools from 19 studies by whether they support generative or exploratory processes, in eight support dimensions. AI tools and traditional tools form a continuum.
numbers: 57 tools, 19 studies; 61.4% of tools support generation, 38.6% support exploration.
limits: Qualitative content analysis, not an outcome study; no tests of effect.
agent_relevance: Tools lean toward generation and under-serve exploration. Our scaffold's value may lie on the exploration side.

source: Generating preinventive structures: AI-driven creativity in product repurposing (ICED 2025, Cambridge University Press, doi 10.1017/pds.2025.10207)
finding: Directly casts an LLM step as generating preinventive structures. GPT-4o was given the Geneplore definition and a drawing of an IKEA LACK table and asked for structures from table components, without solutions. These were compared with structures reverse-identified from real IKEA hacks.
numbers: GPT-4o produced 7 structures: shelving unit (21 hacks), partition wall (8), flat surface module (6), trestle bridge (6), leg framework (2), modular cubes (1), platform staircase (1). 49 hacks met the inclusion rules; 12 contained structures not in the AI list.
limits: One product, one model, one prompt; coverage by label only, with no novelty or usefulness scoring; single coder.
agent_relevance: Gives an LLM analogue of a preinventive structure: a component-combination description with no function yet. Coverage of 37 of 49 hacks shows the generator finds the common ones; the uncommon human ones are the gap.

source: Smith et al. (1993) and Marsh et al. (1996), joint reading: what an example constraint does
finding: Across the two experiment series, examples raise feature overlap with the examples (.11 to .24 and .22 to .35 in Smith; .087 to .280 from 0 to 9 examples in Marsh) without clear loss in total output (about 3 vs 3 items in Smith; 4.4 to 5.4 items in Marsh). Constraint changes what is made, not clearly how much.
numbers: Not a statistical meta-analysis; numbers taken from two papers read in full.
limits: Different example sets, scoring and judges; the comparison is informal.
agent_relevance: Constraints are safe to use as a test (S4) to shape output; the main cost is overlap, not volume.
